overview:
Denmark is the smallest and southernmost of the Scandinavian countries, made up of the Jutland peninsula, which points north from Germany, and about 400 islands, of which around 70 are inhabited. The mainland part is about twice the size of Massachusetts. The capital, Copenhagen, spreads across two islands and is famous for its harbor, colorful waterfront houses, and streets where bicycles outnumber cars. The Kingdom of Denmark also includes two self-governing territories, Greenland and the Faroe Islands.

About 6 million people live in Denmark and speak Danish. It is a constitutional monarchy, with one of the oldest royal families in the world and a parliament that makes the laws. Danes pay high taxes and in return receive free schooling, university, and health care, and they regularly rank among the happiest people on Earth. The country produces wind turbines, medicines, and famous design, and it is home to LEGO bricks, fairy tales by Hans Christian Andersen, and the cozy way of life Danes call hygge.
landAndNature: Denmark is flat and low; its highest natural point, Møllehøj, rises only 171 meters, and no place is far from the sea. The coastline stretches more than 7,000 kilometers if all the islands are counted, with sandy beaches on the west coast pounded by North Sea waves and gentler shores facing the Baltic. Farmland covers more than half the country, with fields of wheat, barley, and rapeseed and countless pig farms. At Skagen, the northern tip, two seas meet and their waves visibly collide. The chalk cliffs of Møns Klint gleam white above the sea, and the Wadden Sea mudflats host millions of migrating birds. Red deer roam the heaths of Jutland, and seals rest on sandbanks. The climate is mild, windy, and often cloudy.
peopleAndCulture: Danes value trust, equality, and hygge, the warm coziness of candles, good food, and friends on a dark winter evening. Nearly half of Copenhagen residents cycle to work or school along wide bike lanes. Open-faced sandwiches called smørrebrød, piled with herring, egg, or roast pork on dark rye bread, are a lunchtime classic, and flaky pastries known abroad as Danish are called wienerbrød at home. Handball and soccer are the top sports; Denmark won the 1992 European soccer championship as a last-minute replacement team. The author Hans Christian Andersen wrote The Little Mermaid and The Ugly Duckling, philosopher Søren Kierkegaard and physicist Niels Bohr were Danish, and Danish furniture and architecture set world styles in the 20th century.
history: Farmers settled Denmark after the last Ice Age, and around the year 800 the Vikings sailed from its shores to raid and trade across Europe, ruling parts of England for a time. King Harald Bluetooth united the country and brought Christianity around 965. In the Middle Ages Denmark ruled Norway and, for a while, Sweden, and it kept Norway until 1814. Denmark became a constitutional monarchy in 1849. It lost territory to Prussia in 1864 but stayed neutral in World War I. Nazi Germany occupied Denmark from 1940 to 1945, and in 1943 Danes secretly ferried almost all of the country's Jews to safety in Sweden. Denmark joined NATO in 1949 and the European Union in 1973, though it kept its own currency.
funFacts: LEGO bricks were invented in the Danish town of Billund, and the name combines the Danish words for play well.
The Bluetooth wireless symbol is made from the runic initials of Viking king Harald Bluetooth.
Denmark's flag, a white cross on red, is considered the oldest national flag still in use, dating to the 1300s.
Copenhagen has more bicycles than people, and about 45 percent of residents commute by bike.
The Øresund Bridge and tunnel link Denmark to Sweden across 16 kilometers of sea, carrying cars and trains.
